raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old woman presented to our primary care clinic with tender, subcutaneous nodules on her right ankle and right thigh of 2 months duration. The lesions had begun as 1-2 mm reddish papules that progressed into 2-3 cm nodules. She denied insect bites, local trauma, or the use of new cosmetic products. The previous month she had visited our emergency department complaining of the lesions, and she was at that time treated for presumed cellulitis with a 7-day course of clindamycin, without improvement.
Her medical history consisted of well-controlled asthma. Her only medication was inhaled albuterol. She had received a Bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccine during childhood. She had emigrated from China 20 years ago. Her husband had been successfully treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 30 years ago. She herself had never received a diagnosis of latent or active tuberculosis. She had no history of substance abuse.
Physical examination revealed three dusky, reddish, ill-defined, edematous subcutaneous nodules (2-3 cm) proximal to her right medial malleolus (Fig. 1). The lesions were slightly tender and cool to touch. There were subcentimeter lesions of similar appearance scattered along the medial right thigh. There was no lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.
Bacterial and fungal infections, vasculitis, thrombophlebitis, erythema nodosum, and sarcoid were considered in the differential diagnosis. A complete blood count, basic serum chemistry, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal. Serum complement levels and serologies for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, antineutrophil antibodies, and rheumatoid factor were normal. Antibodies to hepatitis B and C and HIV were negative. A plain film of the chest was normal. The excisional biopsy of one of the lesions revealed granulomas in the subcutaneous fat, surrounded by fibrosis and reactive changes (Fig. 2). At this point, cutaneous tuberculosis was suspected. An interferon gamma release assay was positive for M. tuberculosis, signifying infection. However, mycobacterial staining and culture of tissue for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) were negative. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) applied to the tissue failed to detect M. tuberculosis DNA. Bacterial and fungal cultures of tissue were also negative. A CT scan of the thorax to evaluate for occult pulmonary tuberculosis was normal.
We decided to treat the patient for presumptive cutaneous tuberculosis because of the histopathologic findings of granulomas in the setting of the patient's immigration from an endemic area, history of exposure to active tuberculosis (spouse), and positive interferon gamma release assay. Eight weeks after beginning treatment with pyrazinamide, rifampin, ethambutol, and isoniazid, the lesions had completely resolved. The patient received a total of 9 months of treatment and has had no recurrence during 3 years of follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old female presented with tender subcutaneous nodules on her right ankle and right thigh of 2 months duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 57-year-old female noticed 1-2 mm reddish papules on her right medial ankle and right thigh 2 months prior to presentation that progressed into 2-3 cm tender subcutaneous nodules. She had presented to the emergency department one month earlier and received a 7-day course of oral clindamycin for presumed cellulitis without improvement. She denied insect bites, local trauma, or application of new cosmetics.
subjective.past_medical_history: Well-controlled asthma. Emigrated from China 20 years ago. Childhood BCG vaccination. Husband successfully treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 30 years ago. No personal history of active or latent tuberculosis. Treated with a 7-day course of clindamycin without response. Denied substance abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for tender skin nodules. Negative for fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, respiratory symptoms, or arthralgia. Current medication: inhaled albuterol. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Three dusky, reddish, ill-defined, edematous subcutaneous nodules (2-3 cm) proximal to right medial malleolus, slightly tender and cool to touch; scattered subcentimeter dusky nodules along medial right thigh. No lymphadenopathy. Remainder of physical examination normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count, basic serum chemistry, and ESR normal. Serum complement, ANCA, ANA, and rheumatoid factor normal. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV serologies negative. Plain chest radiograph normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Excisional biopsy of skin nodule: granulomatous inflammation in subcutaneous adipose tissue surrounded by fibrosis and reactive changes. Thorax CT: normal lung parenchyma, excluding occult pulmonary tuberculosis. Bacterial and fungal tissue cultures negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Cutaneous tuberculosis (erythema induratum of Bazin / nodular tuberculid), diagnosed based on characteristic histopathology showing subcutaneous granulomatous panniculitis, a positive interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA / QuantiFERON), epidemiological exposure (immigration from endemic region and spousal history of pulmonary TB), and exclusion of alternative etiologies. Tissue AFB staining, AFB culture, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR were negative. Differentials ruled out included bacterial/fungal cellulitis, vasculitis, thrombophlebitis, erythema nodosum, and sarcoidosis. Management & Outcome: Initiated on 4-drug antituberculous therapy (pyrazinamide, rifampin, ethambutol, isoniazid). Lesions completely resolved after 8 weeks. Completed 9 months of therapy with no recurrence during 3 years of follow-up.
